summary: Describes three trust models and the threats relevant to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. It notes that IPsec AH was prescribed but limited to manual keying. The goal is to define requirements for securing Neighbor Discovery. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Computers on a local network ask each other who is who, and liars could answer. This describes who to trust and what attackers could try.

questions: what are the neighbor discovery trust models
how can neighbor discovery be attacked
why not use ipsec ah for neighbor discovery
subtitle: Three ways to think about who you can trust on a local IPv6 link, and the catalog of Neighbor Discovery attacks each one faces.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and address autoconfiguration let nodes learn the local topology, but anyone on the link can send fake messages. The suggested fix, IPsec AH, had no workable key management.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three trust models (corporate intranet, operator-run public network, ad hoc network) and walks through each known threat, showing which models it affects and whether a solution is known.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document for the SEND working group, not a protocol. Several attacks, especially in ad hoc networks, are labeled open research problems.

today: RFC 3756 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the trust models and threat catalog that SEND was meant to address, and is not itself a protocol.

sections.title: Why Neighbor Discovery Needs Securing
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 2461) and Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 2462) let nodes learn the local topology: the IP to MAC address mappings of neighbors, the routers on the link, and the prefixes those routers serve.

Those specifications suggest protecting the messages with IPsec AH (RFC 2402) but do not say how. The Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) working group was chartered in Fall 2002 to define protection without excessive manual keying. This document supplies the groundwork: the kinds of networks the solution must work in and the threats it must address.

It is explicit that its discussion of example solutions, such as Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGA) and Address Based Keys (ABK), is only illustrative and shows no preference.
sections.eli5: Neighbors on a street need to know who lives where. This note says: before we invent a lock, let us first list who might cheat and in what kinds of streets.

sections.title: Why IPsec AH Was Not Enough
sections.content:
The original ND and autoconfiguration RFCs recommended IPsec AH but left key management for future work. The RFC explains why that oversimplifies things.

  • A host joining a public network may have no security association with it, and a roaming user is unlikely to have a pre-set trust relationship with a foreign provider.
  • ND is used to get initial access to a link, so any security association would have to be fully preconfigured by hand.
  • The key agreement protocol IKE has a chicken-and-egg problem: you need an IP address to run IKE, IKE is needed to set up IPsec SAs, and the SAs are needed to configure an IP address.
  • ND uses a range of 16 million solicited node multicast addresses, so preconfigured SAs for all of them would be unmanageable.
sections.eli5: The lock people suggested needed a key, but you need to already be inside the house to get the key. That does not work for someone just arriving.

sections.title: The Three Trust Models
sections.content:
The word "trust" here is used non-technically: it means a shared organizational belief about how other parties will behave. The RFC splits the ND mechanisms into Neighbor Discovery (operations not primarily involving routers) and Router Discovery (those that do), then defines three models.

  1. Corporate intranet. All authenticated nodes are under one administration and trust each other not to send false ND or RD messages. If the link is physically secure or cryptographically protected (for example 802.1x wired access control or 802.11i RSN), no extra protection is needed unless a node is compromised. ND security still adds depth, limiting damage from a compromised node.
  2. Public network with an operator. Clients trust the operator's router to forward faithfully and not send false ND or RD messages, but clients do not trust each other. Link-layer security does not block every threat, since 802.11i broadcast and multicast keys are shared among all nodes, and the access point may be invisible at the IP layer.
  3. Ad hoc network. No node trusts any other, and there are no trusted third parties, so traditional authentication does not work. Self-identifying mechanisms such as CGA can at least show that a node generated its own address and is the same node as before.
sections.eli5: Imagine three places: a school where everyone knows each other, a cafe where you trust the owner but not the other customers, and a street party full of strangers. How much you can believe people is different in each.

sections.title: Neighbor and Address Threats
sections.content:
The RFC groups threats into redirect attacks, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks and flooding DoS attacks. The first group does not involve routers.

  • NS/NA spoofing (4.1.1). An attacker sends a Neighbor Solicitation or Advertisement with a different link-layer address, so the Neighbor Cache entry is overwritten and packets go elsewhere. If it keeps answering the Neighbor Unreachability Detection probes, the redirect persists. Using an unused address only lasts 30-50 seconds with default timers.
  • NUD failure (4.1.2). A malicious node keeps sending fabricated Neighbor Advertisements in reply to NUD probes to prolong an attack.
  • DAD DoS (4.1.3). An attacker answers every Duplicate Address Detection attempt, claiming the address, so a joining host never obtains one.

None of these is a concern in the intranet model unless a node is compromised. In the operator model the router may act as a trusted proxy certifying bindings, and in the ad hoc model self-certifying techniques such as CGA may be used. The RFC cautions that limiting how many addresses a host may use could be harmful, since one node may legitimately want many.
sections.eli5: A cheater tells everyone "that kid's mail should come to me," or shouts "that seat is taken!" every time someone tries to sit down. This section lists those tricks.

sections.title: Router and Routing Threats
sections.content:
These threats target Router Discovery and router-assisted mechanisms.

  • Malicious last hop router (4.2.1). An attacker sends Router Advertisements to pose as a router, even advertising the real router with a lifetime of zero, to siphon traffic or mount a man-in-the-middle attack. RFC 2462 partially mitigates this for prefix lifetimes, but default router selection in RFC 2461 has no such rule.
  • Default router killed (4.2.2). If the Default Router List is empty a sender assumes the destination is on-link, which lets the attacker use NS/NA spoofing even against off-link destinations.
  • Good router goes bad (4.2.3). A trusted router is compromised. No known solutions exist for any trust model.
  • Spoofed Redirect (4.2.4). The attacker uses the first-hop router's link-local address to send a Redirect to a host.
  • Bogus on-link prefix (4.2.5). A host believing a prefix is on-link never sends it to the router, so its Neighbor Solicitations go unanswered. One suggested limit is to require advertised on-link prefixes to be /64s.
  • Bogus address configuration prefix (4.2.6). A host builds an address from an invalid prefix, and replies never reach it. The harm can spread through dynamic DNS updates.
  • Parameter spoofing (4.2.7). A forged Router Advertisement sets a tiny Current Hop Limit or sets the M or O flag to point hosts at a bogus DHCPv6 server.
sections.eli5: Here the cheater pretends to be the crossing guard. They can send people the wrong way, say the real guard went home, or give wrong instructions.

sections.title: Replay, Remote Attacks and the Summary
sections.content:
Two further threats cut across the models. Replay attacks (4.3.1) apply to all ND and RD messages, even cryptographically protected ones, so any securing mechanism must resist replay. The RFC notes they are fairly easy to defeat: nonces in request-reply exchanges, and timestamps or counters for stand-alone messages such as unsolicited Advertisements or Redirects.

The Neighbor Discovery DoS attack (4.3.2) has an attacker, possibly off-link, send packets to many fabricated addresses with the right subnet prefix. The last hop router keeps sending Neighbor Solicitations and its neighbor cache fills up. The RFC compares it to TCP SYN flooding and suggests rate limiting, limiting state for unresolved solicitations and careful cache management.

Section 4.4 tabulates all attacks per trust model with a minus sign (not present or not a concern), a plus sign (present, a solution is known in principle) and the letter R (present, solving it is a research problem). The ad hoc column is mostly R for the router threats. The RFC's own Security Considerations section says only that the document is concerned entirely with security.
sections.eli5: A cheater can also record a real message and play it back later, or flood the guard with fake questions until nobody else gets help. The answer keys at the end say which tricks we know how to stop.
